The game semantics of Chapter~\ref{ch:game_theory} gives the stopping instance a second, complementary reading. Building on the \ac{relu}-network games of \textcite{Gaubert2025}, the stopping decomposition was reinterpreted as a two-player zero-sum \ac{sg} on a doubled state graph: weight signs route between the players $P^+$ and $P^-$, gradients and $\alpha\beta$-\ac{lrp} attributions emerge as discounted occupation measures under equilibrium policies, and the deformation parameters of Chapter~\ref{ch:decompositions} --- temperature, risk aversion, stabilizers --- become principled modifications of the game. Chapter~\ref{ch:trajectory} takes the decisive step: the equilibrium policies induce a genuine \emph{probability distribution} $\Pi$ over complete backward trajectories, and this distribution --- not any pixel-space projection --- is the backward computation. The comparison with the \ac{nrm} framework of \textcite{Xiong2026nrm} in Section~\ref{sec:nrm_comparison} identifies their shared path perspective: \ac{nrm} assigns normalized signed relevance to neuron walks, while the game separates a probability law on expanded states from the signs and discounts used to recover attribution. A direct identification requires matching the propagation and normalization conventions. The probability law makes trajectory-level statistical comparison possible: the Hellinger distance between two backward computations is computable in one linear-time pass, and the parameter-randomization sanity check of \textcite{Adebayo2018sanity} lifts from attribution maps to trajectory space, where Theorem~\ref{thm:rand_stopping} shows Bhattacharyya mass decays geometrically in the number of randomized layers --- detecting collapse even when heatmaps remain deceptively similar \parencite{sixt2020whenexplanationslie}.

The discounted occupation measures at the input layer recover gradient and $\alpha\beta$-\ac{lrp} maps (Theorems~\ref{ptnb:thm:deriv-occ} and~\ref{ptnb:thm:ab-recovery}). The undiscounted endpoint marginal $m^{(0)}_M$ is generally different: Hellinger compares the trajectory routing laws and does not include the path discounts. Theorems~\ref{ptnb:thm:rand-adf}--\ref{ptnb:thm:rand-routing} show that $\Pi_M$ changes drastically under randomization, while Table~\ref{tab:sanity-check} shows that the resulting attribution maps can remain similar. \ch{The two
diagnostics therefore detect different aspects of parameter sensitivity: the map-level test
of~\textcite{Adebayo2018sanity} asks whether the explanation delivered to the user depends on the
learned parameters, the trajectory-level test whether the calculation behind it does. A map can fail
the first while its calculation passes the second; the trajectory-level result locates where the
sensitivity is lost (between the calculation and its pixel projection), but it does not make such a
map adequate for model debugging~\parencite{Adebayo2018sanity,sixt2020whenexplanationslie}.}
